articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq fall as Alphabet stock sell-off drags on tech, AI jitters return
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq fall as Alphabet stock sell-off drags on tech, AI jitters return
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks fell at the open on Thursday as Alphabet's Q3 earnings sparked a sell-off in the stock and AI jitters returned to markets, dragging on the tech-heavy indexes.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 0.1%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) lost 0.3%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell 1.2%.
Tech stocks snapped a positive run this week as investors digested the Fed's rate pause on Wednesday and earnings from Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ). Microsoft beat analyst expectations on the top and bottom lines, while Alphabet sales came up short . Although Google posted cloud growth of 103%, concerns about its free cash flow and AI return on investment were the albatross on the company's quarter.
A sell-off in AI names spread, as the iShares Semiconductor Index ETF ( SOXX ) skidded and software stocks ( IGV ) also tumbled, with double-digit losses for Fortinet ( FTNT ) and ServiceNow ( NOW ) following their earnings reports.
Markets will get another dose of hyperscaler earnings after the bell on Thursday when Amazon ( AMZN ) reports results. Several other stocks were moving in premarket trading on individual earnings: Eli Lilly ( LLY ), for example, popped 4% following strong Q3 results for its GLP-1 drugs.
Thursday's market action comes after the Federal Reserve held rates unchanged on Wednesday afternoon. The decision had two dissenters who favored a rate hike amid sticky inflation. Meanwhile, a fresh reading of the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up in September, with the Personal Consumption Expenditures index rising 3.6% year over year.
In other news, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said on Thursday she will leave her post on Feb. 7, 2027, months ahead of schedule. The early departure comes at a delicate time for Europe, which continues to battle persistent inflation, surging bond yields, and domestic unrest in France over ballooning deficits and proposed austerity measures.
Shares of Sprout's Farmers Market ( SFM ) plunged 19% Thursday after the grocery chain cut its profit outlook and announced aggressive price cuts in a bid to win back shoppers.
The Phoenix, Ariz.-based specialty supermarket is embarking on a price-slashing strategy that's now expected to weigh on profits into next year as it's seeing fewer customers.
"We do not expect a smooth road ahead," JPMorgan analyst Thomas Palmer wrote to clients Thursday, describing the earnings reduction as "massive" but keeping its "overweight" rating on the grocery chain.
After warning about third quarter earnings, Sprouts told analysts on Tuesday it expects Q4 earnings of between $0.47 and $0.51 per share, well below the $1.21 analysts had anticipated, according to S&P Global data.
The company cited increasingly price-sensitive customers, along with this year's outbreak of the foodborne parasite cyclospora, as key headwinds driving the sales decline. It's also in the midst of a CEO transition after Sprouts announced last month that COO Nicholas Konat will take over for current CEO Jack Sinclair in early January.
Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger reports:
A fresh reading of the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up in September, solidifying expectations for an interest rate hike in December.
The Personal Consumption Expenditures index rose 3.6%, in line with expectations and up from 3.4% a month earlier. On a core basis, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, PCE rose 3.1%, also in line with expectations and up a tenth of a percentage point from 3% in August. Month over month, core PCE clocked in at 0.3%, in line with projections, marking a faster pace from the 0.2% seen in August.
The data was anticipated, prompting many analysts to feel a rate hike was in order Wednesday, given other inflation readings ahead of the Fed's meeting that showed price increases last month.
Yahoo Finance's Molly Moorhead reports:
The US economy grew at a robust pace in the third quarter, driven by investment, consumer spending, and government spending.
Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4% annualized rat e, according to an initial estimate released Thursday by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis, beating economists' expectations of 3.1% and marking an acceleration from the second quarter's 2.2% growth.
Third-quarter growth was partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are subtracted in the calculation of GDP, increased. The artificial intelligence build-out was the main engine, with business investment surging 12.7%. Consumer spending grew 3.8%, matching the rate in Q2 and the strongest since the end of 2024.
Alphabet ( GOOGL ) is on track for its worst day ever. The stock fell about 13% Thursday after its third quarter results , steeper than any session since it went public in 2004.
That puts nearly $500 billion of stock market value on the line, the second-biggest one-day loss ever for a US-listed company. Only Nvidia ( NVDA ) has lost more, about $593 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, the day China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors.
Alphabet would need to close at about $274.75, down roughly 15%, to take Nvidia's record, by Yahoo Finance calculations. It has already blown past the $400 billion SpaceX ( SPCX ) lost on June 22, the previous No. 2.
US stocks opened lower Thursday after disappointing earnings from industry giant Alphabet ( GOOGL ) dragged down indexes.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 0.6%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) lost 0.5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell 1.4%.
Alphabet stock sank after its quarterly sales disappointed , while Microsoft ( MSFT ) held up better following its report.
The moves come as investors continue to scrutinize whether massive spending on artificial intelligence is translating quickly enough into earnings growth across Big Tech.
DoorDash ( DASH ) announced plans to acquire hyper-local grocery delivery provider Instacart ( CART ) on Thursday morning in a deal valued at $17 billion.
DoorDash, which is primarily known for its restaurant food delivery business, will pay $65 per Instacart share, a 26% premium over the stock's Oct. 22 closing price. The transaction includes 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both. Instacart's board of directors unanimously approved the deal, according to a press release.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online," DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the release. "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."
DoorDash stock popped over 5% in premarket trading, while Instacart stock edged lower.
Marvell Technology ( MRVL ) stock dropped 11% on Thursday on reports that the AI chipmaker is in advanced talks to purchase optical parts maker Lumentum ( LITE ). Shares of Lumentum surged 5%.
The potential multibillion-dollar mega deal between the semiconductor designer and Lumentum was first reported by Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.
An agreement could be announced as soon as next week. Lumentum has a market value of about $83 billion, compared with Marvell's roughly $221 billion.
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban reports:
Retail investors are changing the way they trade.
While overall retail volumes are declining , as Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider wrote in a recent note, money is shifting away from traditional equities.
Instead, more investors are pouring their funds into options, leveraged ETFs, and prediction markets. Robinhood's ( HOOD ) latest earnings offer a window into the shift .
The online brokerage reported weaker-than-expected profits earlier this week as declining interest income and rising expenses weighed on the company. But it also drew record tr

articles.title_orig: U.S. GDP Increased 3.4% in Third Quarter
articles.title_zh: U.S. GDP Increased 3.4% in Third Quarter
articles.content_orig:
The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday.
The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below.
Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends.
While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter.
GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter.
Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%.
The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move.
"The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that's happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday.
However, the data deluge from Thursday shows the Fed could have more work to do.
A Labor Department report also released Thursday showed that layoffs remain low. Initial jobless claims edged lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the estimate for 200,000 and near levels last seen in the late 1960s.
Stock market future s were negative following the releases while Treasury yields also fell.
"Net, net, economic growth is powering ahead despite the uncertainty of geopolitical risks and the damage posed to many sectors of the economy by higher energy costs," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "The economy was thought to have been a lost cause during much of the current Administration's time in office, but real GDP has bounced back above a 3 percent run rate in Q3 2026 for the first time in a year."
Economic growth has been driven by higher levels of investment from the artificial intelligence build-out, as well as high levels of consumer and government spending.
Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the third quarter, the same pace as the prior period. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% jump on intellectual property products.
Real sales to private domestic purchasers, a proxy that Fed officials use for underlying demand, rose 4.9%, compared with a 4.6% increase in the second quarter.
There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter.
September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%.
At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

articles.title_orig: China's Communist Party conclave on toughening discipline sees record expulsions, absences
articles.title_zh: China's Communist Party conclave on toughening discipline sees record expulsions, absences
articles.content_orig:
This is the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Analysts believe one reason for the increased empahsis on discipline â which many interpret as loyalty â is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."
'Tigers and flies': Millions of officials later, why is Xi's corruption purge still going?

articles.title_orig: Israelis await final election results as claim of foreign interference emerges
articles.title_zh: Israelis await final election results as claim of foreign interference emerges
articles.content_orig:
Netanyahu’s claim of interference in election also dismissed by Israeli police and opposition parties
Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition
Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman rejected accusations “made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media” that his country had interfered in the Israeli elections.
“We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome,” Majed al-Ansari said on X.
“They accuse Qatar of buying off Benjamin Netanyahu , the Israeli political left and now, in this latest campaign, the Arab vote... These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure.”
Mahmoud Abbas, the president of the Palestinian Authority, expressed hope that the Israeli election would pave the way for renewed peace talks.
“For many years now, we have been extending a hand to the Israeli side in order to achieve peace with them, so that Israel and Palestine may live in security, stability and peace,” Abbas said during a meeting with Cypriot president Nikos Christodoulides in Nicosia.
“We hope that, immediately after a new Israeli government is formed, we will be able to engage in dialogue together.”
As vote counting continues in Israel , here is a roundup of today’s key developments:
Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have amplified allegations of election fraud against parties representing Palestinian citizens in Israel. He and members of his coalition have referred the parties to Shin Bet, the country’s domestic security service, for investigation. Netanyahu’s Likud party accused the Palestinian parties of “stealing” the election and claimed, without evidence, that they received money from Qatar.
Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, rejected the allegations, saying they were “ridiculous and dangerous”. Responding to the claims, he said: “We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome.”
The Israeli president, Isaac Herzog, has come to the defence of Palestinian voters, as he urged political leaders against “tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote”. He said Shin Bet and the country’s central elections committee would investigate allegations of foreign interference “throughly”.
The central elections committee’s acting director general, Dean Livne, said there was “no basis for claims of systematic violations of election integrity”. The Israeli police also dismissed the claims, according to comments reported in Hebrew-language media, with one source quoted as saying: “Election day passed with very few irregular incidents.”
Netanyahu’s chief rival, former military chief and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, warned political opponents against exploiting allegations of foreign interference to delay the swearing-in of the next Knesset, which is set for 10 November.
The sentiment was shared by Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, who accused Netanyahu of trying to “undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimisation campaign” targeting Palestinian citizens in Israel.
So far, Netanyahu’s bloc is projected to win 53 seats , compared with 48 for the grouping led by rival Eisenkot . Palestinian parties are projected to win 19 seats , a record high.
The final tally of absentee ballots is not expected to significantly shift the results, with no grouping managing to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman rejected accusations “made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media” that his country had interfered in the Israeli elections.
“We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome,” Majed al-Ansari said on X.
“They accuse Qatar of buying off Benjamin Netanyahu , the Israeli political left and now, in this latest campaign, the Arab vote... These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure.”
Both Benjamin Netanyahu and his immediate challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, lack the seats in the Knesset to form a majority government. Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice.
They could forge a pact with the Arab Israeli parties, currently heading for an historic 19 seats, which would allow them to vote Netanyahu out and form a governing coalition. Or they could enter a unity government with Netanyahu, in return for a ministry or two.
Likud officials are cited in today’s Israeli press as saying Eisenkot will ultimately have no option but to throw in his lot with Netanyahu. Other observers say that would be political suicide, especially as the opposition leader vowed in the campaign he would never collaborate with the prime minister.
However, Eisenkot and key members of his bloc have also ruled out cooperation with the Arab party lists. Breaking either pledge would be costly for them.
The prime minister’s attack on the legitimacy of the Palestinian vote is designed to tip the scales, to force Eisenkot into the Netanyahu camp by increasing the political toxicity of any arrangement with Arab parties, the Joint List and Ra’am.
For its part, the Joint List has ruled out participating in an Eisenkot government because of his bloc’s support for the war in Gaza and the occupation of southern Lebanon, but it has offered to support an Eisenkot minority government with tactical voting in the new Knesset, in the shared interest of ousting Netanyahu.
Even such a transactional arrangement is hard to achieve given the state of Israeli Jewish politics. The only Zionist party that advocates cooperation with Palestinians, the Democrats, won just 6.5% of the total vote by the latest count.
The right and centre-right accounted for 66.5%, while ultra-orthodox Jewish parties won 11%.
Against that background, Eisenkot has doubled down on his determination to form a Zionist government. Such rhetoric makes the prospect of cooperation with Arab parties even more remote, but he is hoping instead to lure away conservative Jews from Likud, just as Netanyahu’s is trawling for defectors from Eisenkot’s “Change” bloc.
This is the current phase of the post-election struggle, and it is one that, for now, excludes Arab Israelis, despite their dramatically increased political strength.
The head of one of Israel’s parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel rejected allegations of electoral fraud and welcomed an investigation, saying his moderate Islamist Ra’am party had “no connection” to the matter.
“Ra’am has no connection whatsoever to the affair in question or to any other affairs, and we declare that we will fully cooperate with all law enforcement authorities to uncover the truth,” Mansour Abbas said, according to a spokesperson for his party.
The race to form a government in Israel has begun with characteristically brass-knuckle tactics from Benjamin Netanyahu . He and other members of his coalition have referred the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, the only part of the opposition which over-performed in Tuesday’s elections, to the country’s domestic security service, the Shin Bet, for investigation.
The government’s claims centre around the allegation that Qatari funds were used illegally to buy votes and mobilise Palestinian Israeli citizens. There is so far no evidence to support the accusation. Haaretz quotes a senior police official saying there were no signs of election fraud and that Tuesday’s vote was cleaner than usual.
In Nazareth on election day, it was clear that turnout was unusually high because of anxiety and fear of what actions the extremists in Netanyahu’s government might turn their attention to Palestinian communities in Israel if they continue in power.

articles.title_orig: Earnings live updates: Eli Lilly stock pops as strong GLP-1 drug demand lifts results, ServiceNow stock plunges
articles.title_zh: Earnings live updates: Eli Lilly stock pops as strong GLP-1 drug demand lifts results, ServiceNow stock plunges
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Third quarter earnings season is in full swing this week, with corporate results dropping from Big Tech heavy-hitters Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).
Read more: Follow Microsoft earnings live updates here.
Aside from Big Tech, industries from oil to chips to pharmaceuticals will be represented, as Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), Intel ( INTC ), Boeing ( BA ), Ford ( F ), and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) also open their books.
It's shaping up to be another strong earnings season. According to FactSet data , nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings so far, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.
Caterpillar ( CAT ) reported and a record order backlog of $78.1 billion in the third quarter, but the stock fell 11% in premarket trading as Wall Street set a high bar and AI-related stocks broadly got hit.
The company has become a growing industrial AI play as its power generation business, which makes and services turbines, has gotten a boost amid booming data center construction.
Here's what Caterpillar reported, versus analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:
Revenue: increased 17% to $20.7 billion, in line with Wall Street estimates.
Adjusted earnings per share: $7.20, versus estimates of $7.03 per share.
Guidance: Maintained full-year outlook for sales to grow in the mid-to-high teens
Analysts may be down on the stock as they were hoping for raised guidance and a wider sales beat.
"Our third-quarter results reflect the durability of our end markets, with strong order rates and a record backlog," Caterpillar CEO Joe Creed said in the release. "Our team continues to execute our strategic priorities in a dynamic environment, positioning us for a strong year while delivering long-term value for our customers and shareholders."
Eli Lilly ( LLY ) shares jumped 4% in premarket trading as strong demand for the company's GLP-1 drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound boosted the company's third quarter results.
Here's what Eli Lilly reported, versus analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:
Revenue: up 39% year over year to $24.4 billion, versus estimates of $22.6 billion
Adjusted earnings per share: up 7% to $7.48, versus estimates of $6.35
Guidance: Increased full-year revenue guidance to a new range of $91 billion to $92 billion
"Revenue growth was driven by broad global consumer demand for Mounjaro and Zepbound, the global launches of Foundayo, expanded U.S. coverage for obesity care and a doubling in our newest products in oncology, immunology and neuroscience," Lilly CEO David Ricks said in the earnings release.
Mounjaro sales rose 65% year over year to $10.7 billion, while Zepbound sales were up 49% to $5.35 billion.
Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) profit took a hit from an unusual place: its stakes in other companies.
Those holdings include about 14% of Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) and a piece of SpaceX ( SPCX ). They supplied about $6 of Alphabet's $9.11 in per-share profit in the second quarter. In the third quarter, a nearly $9 billion loss on them cut earnings by $0.55 a share, to $2.12.
The filing that shows which stakes fell isn't out yet, but SpaceX stock dropped about 12% during the quarter.
Watch Anthropic's IPO, which could start trading as soon as Nov. 16. Once it's public, Alphabet will value that stake at the market price every quarter.
Chipotle ( CMG ) reported third quarter earnings on Wednesday after market close that were better than the Street expected as the restaurant chain sustained sales momentum following slower sales growth since the first quarter of 2025.
Chipotle posted a 2.1% gain in same-store sales, higher than the 1.5% gain Wall Street expected. It posted adjusted earnings of $0.27 per share, slightly below the $0.29 per share expected.
"Three consecutive quarters of positive comparable transaction growth demonstrates that our Recipe for Growth strategy is working," CEO Scott Boatwright wrote in the release, adding that the company saw traction around its menu and digital innovation, high-efficiency equipment rollout and global expansion.
The stock rose 2%. Year to date, shares are down 20%.
ServiceNow ( NOW ) stock plunged 15% after the company missed earnings expectations.
Here's what the enterprise software company reported in Q3, versus analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:
Revenue: $4.1 billion, versus estimates of $4.09 billion
Earnings per share: $0.27, versus estimates of $0.35 per share
Current remaining performance obligations (cRPO): $13.65 billion, representing 20.5% year-over-year growth
Guidance: ServiceNow raised its forecast for 2026 subscription revenues to $15.78 billion to $15.79 billion.
"This was more than another beat-and-raise quarter for ServiceNow, this was the inflection point for ServiceNow as the Super Intelligence Control Tower," CEO Bill McDermott said in the earnings release. "Our customers have validated our strategic relevance as the single harness for enterprise intelligence and security."
Yahoo Finance's Daniel Howley reports:
Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) reported its third quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, missing revenue projections on lower-than-anticipated advertising sales.
Google saw earnings per share (EPS) of $2.12 on revenue of 127.58 billion. Analysts were looking for EPS of $3.01 on revenue of $127.93 billion. Revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs came in at $111.21 billion. Wall Street was anticipating $111.29 billion.
Google's advertising segment saw sales of $82.01 billion versus expectations of $83.5 billion, while its cloud unit brought in $30.71 billion. Analysts were projecting revenue of $29.1 billion.
The results come just hours after the company debuted its latest frontier AI model.
Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
Ford ( F ) reported third quarter earnings that topped estimates and upped the lower end of its profit guidance. The company still sees EV losses piling up by the end of the year.
For the quarter, Ford reported automotive revenue of $46.1 billion vs. $46.2 billion, per Bloomberg consensus, with adjusted EPS of $0.49 vs. $0.41, and adjusted EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) of $2.66 billion vs. $2.38 billion.
Ford tightened the low end of its full-year adjusted EBIT guidance to between $10.5 billion and $11 billion (from $10 billion to $11 billion seen prior); analysts projected full-year adjusted EBIT of $10.52 billion. Ford's adjusted free cash flow guidance remained at $6 billion to $7 billion.
Vertiv ( VRT ) stock surged 15% in premarket trading as the data center infrastructure player showed it continues to benefit from the massive capex spending from the likes of Google ( GOOG ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ).
"We are in the middle of the largest infrastructure buildout and it's accelerating," Vertiv's CEO Giordano Albertazzi said. "The demands on data center infrastructure are evolving faster than ever, and Vertiv's role in that buildout keeps expanding."
Vertiv makes power and cooling hardware for data centers and enterprise networks. As AI fuels demand for this infrastructure, Vertiv said its orders have doubled year over year. The company counts Alphabet, Microsoft, Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) among its customers, per S&P Global Market Intelligence.
That demand, plus strong third quarter results, have given Vertiv the confidence to raise its full-year outlook. In 2026, the company expects net sales of $14.45 billion to $14.85 billion, up from $13.8 billion to $14.2 billion.
Adjusted diluted earnings per share are expected to be $7.10-$7.20 for the year, representing earnings growth of 69%-71%. The midpoint of that range is above the $6.73 per share forecast Wall Street analysts penciled in.
In the third quarter, Vertiv reported net sales of $4.31 billion, beating Wall Street's expectations of $3.76 billion. Adjust

articles.title_orig: SNAPSHOT US stock index futures pare losses after economic data
articles.title_zh: SNAPSHOT US stock index futures pare losses after economic data
articles.content_orig:
iCapital chief investment strategist Sonali Basak joins Making Money to discuss the Federal Reserve holding interest rates steady, two dissenting FOMC votes and the economy continuing to expand at a strong pace.
This story about the September 2026 PCE inflation report will be updated with further details.
The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge rose further away from the central bank's target in September as consumers face price pressures.
The Commerce Department on Thursday reported that the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index rose 0.5% on a monthly basis in September and was up 3.6% from a year ago. Both figures were in line with the expectations of economists polled by LSEG.
Core PCE, which excludes volatile measurements of food and energy prices, was up 0.3% on a monthly basis and 3.1% year over year. Those figures were both in line with economists' expectations.
Federal Reserve policymakers are focused on the PCE headline figure as they try to bring inflation back to their long-run target of 2%, though they view core data as a better indicator of inflation.
Compared with August's readings, headline PCE ticked up from 3.4% to 3.6%, while core PCE rose from 3% to 3.1%.
Goods prices were up 3.9% year over year, while services prices increased 3.5% from a year ago in September.
The personal savings rate as a percentage of disposable personal income was 3.8%, down from 4% in August.
Over the last two years, the savings rate has declined from a peak of 6.2% in April 2025 and from 5.6% in January 2026.
While inflation moved further away from the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also released the advance estimate for third quarter gross domestic product (GDP) which grew more than expected.
The Bureau of Economic Analysis estimated that third quarter GDP was 3.4%, above the 3.2% estimate of economists polled by LSEG. The BEA will release two subsequent revisions of the Q3 GDP data.

articles.title_orig: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion in big consolidation for grocery delivery
articles.title_zh: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion in big consolidation for grocery delivery
articles.content_orig:
DoorDash is buying rival Instacart in a deal worth roughly $17 billion, signaling that the delivery wars continue to heat up.
The deal, announced Thursday, marks an end for Instacart as an independent company. Instacart went public in 2023 and benefited from a pandemic-era boom for the grocery delivery service, but it has struggled to maintain its momentum against larger competitors, like Uber, Amazon and Walmart.
Combining Instacart and DoorDash would create a larger company that better competes with those rivals. Amazon, for example continues to expand its same-day grocery service , which now totals 2,300 locations, while Walmart now offers 30 minute delivery in some places. Meanwhile, Uber has expanded its offerings, recently inking a deal with Costco.
DoorDash said in a press release that the combined company “will offer grocers and retailers of every size DoorDash’s delivery network and Instacart’s grocery and fulfillment technology.”
DoorDash has been expanding its suite of services beyond meal delivery, including adding restaurant reservations and delivery products beyond food, striking partnerships with Home Depot and Sephora. Now, it can increase its business with more grocery options, too.
“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Tony Xu, the cofounder and CEO of DoorDash said in a statement.
He added that Instacart “has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”
The deal is a mix of cash and stock, with DoorDash paying $65 per share, marking a roughly 25% premium from Instacart’s October 22 close when media reports said that it was mulling a sale.
The companies are touting the benefits of the combination, including that people won’t have to buy two membership programs (DashPass and Instacart+), which could save its customers an “estimated $100 million per year on membership fees alone.”
But there’s already opposition to the deal, with the American Economic Liberties Project (AELP), an anti-monopoly advocacy group, pushing regulators to block the deal because it would control nearly 60% of the third-party grocery delivery market.
“Instacart and Doordash have spent the better part of a decade bullying main street businesses and denying fair pay and benefits to their combined 9 million workers,” said Lee Hepner, Senior Legal Counsel at the AELP, in a statement. “This merger represents the next frontier of data-driven abuse, exploiting massive asymmetries of power to squeeze worker compensation on the way in and drain consumer wallets on the way out.”
The combination, which is expected to close in the coming months, is one of many in the delivery space. Grubhub’s US business was sold to Wonder for $650 million in 2025, and Uber bought European company Delivery Hero this summer for $14.8 billion. In 2020, Uber bought Postmates for $2.65 billion.

articles.title_orig: Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal
articles.title_zh: Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal
articles.content_orig:
For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this coming two-day meeting in Montreal.
Thursday and Friday's summit will be closely watched for details on how Canada  and the European bloc deepen their ties.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.
The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
Von der Leyen, speaking to reporters after landing in Montreal on Wednesday, said the two sides will "start discussing how to make Canada the first associate member of the EU".
"Our ambition is to build the closest partnership we have ever had with a non-European country," she said.
Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship.
Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.
According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".
Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement   last month.
The concept of "associate membership", he added, is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada.
"Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.
Lüttenberg noted, however, that neither Canada nor the EU is seeking full membership for the North American country.
Rather, both want to bring Canada "as close as possible" to the bloc without membership.
On the first day of the summit, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.
Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days.
Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months.
But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic.
Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.
And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties.
"The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit.
Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer.
US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway.
Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme.
It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.
Carney said earlier this week that the summit would "launch further formal discussions" between Canada and the EU on deepening ties and creating new opportunities for both sides.
As for what this new relationship status will be called, the prime minister said the "nomenclature" does not matter.
"What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

articles.title_orig: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
A US cruise ship MV. Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville southern Cambodia, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
A couple passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, stands for an interview with his wife, Lynn Motoya, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

articles.title_orig: Rate decision live: Interest rates held steady in split vote, Warsh says politics played 'no role' ahead of midterm elections
articles.title_zh: Rate decision live: Interest rates held steady in split vote, Warsh says politics played 'no role' ahead of midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Federal Reserve officials voted 10-2 to keep interest rates unchanged, as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike.
The Fed's benchmark rates remained in the 3.75% to 4% range , as widely expected. A rate hike in December, however, appears far more likely, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.
Here are the key takeaways from the Fed's statement and Fed Chairman Warsh's press conference:
Fed upgrades economy from "solid" to "strong": The FOMC updated the language in its statement, adding that "the accumulation of more information will help" it decide the right policy stance. This suggests the Fed is not in a hurry to ease inflation.
But "inflation remains elevated": Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to bringing inflation down to the 2% target. Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , the Fed has positioned itself to continue assessing data.
Warsh announces changes to the Fed's schedule : In 2027, one of the eight Fed meetings will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy with neither a vote on the Fed's funds rate nor a policy statement. In 2028, policymakers will hold two meetings dedicated to strategy and six for setting policy.
Warsh refutes the idea that the decision was politically inflected: Warsh stated that "politics played no role in the decision" — something that generated some discussion with the US midterm elections next week.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he doesn't agree that Fed rate hikes will have no impact on artificial intelligence, given the strong demand for AI and the high returns investors expect.
"I was skeptical of that view," Warsh said during a press conference. "Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything."
Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, in a post last month on X , expressed skepticism that higher rates would reduce demand and investment in AI.
"What if higher rates don't reduce demand and investment because the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates because winning the race for super intelligence has a near infinite ROI and the demand for compute will remain incalculable," Ackman wrote. "What if the old models don't apply to the current paradigm?"
Warsh pointed to how credit spreads for certain assets have widened since the Fed raised rates in September, and financial conditions have tightened as investors have differentiated between tech firms and other companies to invest.
"With respect to the new technology and this investment surge, do interest rates matter? I believe they do," said Warsh. "And I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy."
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh pushed back Wednesday on any suggestion that next week's midterm elections had a role in the Fed's decision to keep interest rates steady . He also dodged multiple questions on political topics and pressure coming his way from the Oval Office.
But it wasn't for a lack of trying from the assembled reporters.
"I appreciate the question, but I'm not going to be responding to quotes from public officials," Warsh said during a press conference when presented with criticisms from President Trump that interest rates should be lower and that his colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee were "political."
When the subject turned to the midterm elections, Warsh was similarly curt.
"Politics played no role in the decision," the chair said, adding, "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
The Warsh Fed's taciturn nature has already raised the stakes for each FOMC meeting. With fewer hints or forward guidance about what the Fed is thinking and planning comes more suspense.
And next year, those stakes will be even higher as the Fed removes a rate decision from its calendar, making each meeting even more important and potentially adding another layer of uncertainty and volatility to markets .
At the October policy meeting on Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced this major change to the Fed's calendar and added that 2028 might feature only six rate decisions. The meetings themselves will remain on the calendar, but instead of the Fed debating rates, broader monetary policy topics will be on the agenda.
Warsh said the reasoning behind the schedule change is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons."
We've all been wondering how the newly installed chair would reshape the Fed. Already, he's been doing that by changing the nature of the Fed's public communication.
Wall Street can't make up its mind about the Fed.
Stocks dipped after the 2 p.m. statement, rallied as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke, then gave much of that back. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is holding a small gain, and chip stocks are doing most of the lifting.
The typical stock isn't doing as well. The equal-weighted S&P 500, which gives every company the same weight, is in the red. So are small caps.
The bond market is clearer about what it thinks. The 30-year Treasury yield is near its high of the day, and the 10-year yield is back above 5%. Higher long-term rates make borrowing more expensive for companies and homebuyers.
The dollar moved the other way and slipped against the euro during the press conference.
That leaves the streak. The S&P 500 came into Wednesday down on six straight Fed days, the second-longest run since 1994, which we pointed out at 2:43 p.m. ET. A higher close would end it, and a lower one would tie the 2018 record of seven.
Chairman Warsh said a couple of words on the Fed's independence amid some discussion that the US midterm elections — just six days away — and the perception that the Fed could influence them could sway the Fed's decision.
"Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh stated. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
"But I will say," Warsh added, "it's an information-rich interval in the coming period, having nothing to do with politics."
The Fed won't be sitting on its hands for long, says the market.
Traders see about an 85% chance that the Fed raises its benchmark rate by a quarter point at its next meeting on Dec. 9, according to Bloomberg data. The data comes from futures contracts that let traders bet on where the Fed sets rates. Those odds are about where they stood Tuesday, before the decision.
Further out, traders expect the Fed's rate to climb from about 3.9% now to nearly 4.7% by September 2027. That's about three more quarter-point hikes, slightly more than they expected Tuesday.
The Dec. 9 meeting is next. A hike would match what traders already expect. Another hold would mean they've gotten ahead of the Fed.
Chairman Warsh noted that while the Fed waits to assess more inflation data, some policymakers view the central bank's moves so far as beginning to take effect.
"If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine starting to work some, but there's no firm conclusions," Warsh said.
"If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he added. "What we decided to do was to call these questions, take stock of where we are, evaluate what we're seeing out the window, ask ourselves whether the period right in front of us is likely to provide more clarity on the appropriate protocol."

articles.title_orig: 2026 Midterm Elections, Oct. 29
articles.title_zh: 2026 Midterm Elections, Oct. 29
articles.content_orig:
On the campaign trail in 2024, President Donald Trump promised to make gas dirt-cheap again and blamed record-high gas prices on the Biden-Harris “war on energy.”
But then an actual war got in the way: Trump’s deeply unpopular conflict with Iran.
Nearly eight months into a war that has destabilized the global energy system, the average price of gas during Trump’s second term is now more expensive than it was during the Biden era, according to a CNN analysis of AAA data.
That milestone — a nearly unthinkable outcome as recently as January — underscores the frustration over high prices that has engulfed Trump and the Republican party leading up to the midterm elections.
“It’s pretty astonishing,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said of the fact that gas is now more expensive under Trump than former President Joe Biden. “I don’t think anyone would have predicted this 10 months ago.”
The difference is tiny – literally a fraction of a penny. As of Tuesday, a gallon of regular gas has averaged $3.473 per gallon since Trump started his second term, compared with $3.471 under Biden.
Are you struggling with high diesel and gas prices? Share your story
Still, the fact these two metrics are even in the same ballpark is a major reversal of the return to sub-$2 gas that Trump promised in the summer of 2024 as he successfully convinced voters to return him to the White House.
And the gap between the Trump and Biden averages is set to grow wider because the national average remains well above $4 a gallon.
During his first term, the national average for regular gas was just $2.47 a gallon. During the depths of the Covid-19 pandemic, gas prices plunged to as low as $1.77 nationally in April 2020.
The health emergency caused demand for fuel to crash to the point that the world ran out of room to store oil, a phenomenon that briefly drove crude oil futures below zero for the first time ever.
At one point in April 2020, Trump even pleaded with Saudi Arabia and Russia to stop pumping so much oil to halt a crash that threatened to bankrupt US oil companies and kill countless jobs.
The situation couldn’t be more different today.
The White House has waged a last-minute scramble to contain the damage from high fuel prices by taking a wide range of steps, including throwing farmers an $8 billion financial lifeline , buying millions of barrels of Russian diesel and examining steps to drive down extremely high shipping costs.
“President Trump is fixing these long-term problems by taking tangible steps to increase our refining capacity here in the United States, while also taking immediate actions, such as releasing oil from our (Strategic Petroleum Reserve) to add supply to the market, temporarily waiving the Jones Act, and allowing red-dyed diesel for highway use, to lower prices at the pump,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told CNN.
The outlook for gasoline and diesel prices was very favorable for Americans when the year started.
Gas prices were safely below $3 a gallon, and, if anything, the energy market was worried about a supply glut that could keep fuel prices low.
“If Trump really wanted to keep his promise to keep gas prices low, what he should have done was nothing,” said Gregory Brew, senior analyst at consulting firm Eurasia Group. “The market was oversupplied. There was a lot of crude sloshing around. Inventories were quite large. But Trump reversed that with the war.”
Trump has argued that elevated gas prices are a small price to pay for keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon.
But the spike in gas prices has angered voters who were hoping for the opposite under Trump.
“High gas prices do not bode well for incumbents. They didn’t bode well for Biden either,” GasBuddy’s De Haan said.
Why gas prices take so long to fall
Gas prices spiked even higher under Biden, zooming to an all-time high of $5.02 a gallon in June 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine.
However, gas prices came down faster under Biden.
In fact, 2026 has already shattered the Biden-era record for the most number of days with $4 gas or higher.
The war with Iran led to the unthinkable: The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway the world relied on to get oil out of the Middle East.
While oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have largely recovered, the cost to get that crude out has skyrocketed because of expensive and inefficient workarounds being used. The cost of hiring an oil tanker has skyrocketed from $65,000 a day last year to $1.6 million earlier this month.
Not only that, but the world is now grappling with a global refining shortage. Refineries that would normally churn out diesel, jet fuel and gasoline have been damaged in the Middle East and Russia. China has held back its own fuel exports.
To make up for lost refinery output, the world has drawn fuel from commercial and emergency stockpiles.
But that leaves the intricate energy system vulnerable to shocks.
Case in point: A recent, unexpected outage at ExxonMobil’s Joliet, Illinois, refinery caused gasoline prices to go through the roof in Michigan, Ohio and other Great Lakes states in recent days.
“Right now, there is no cushion. Commercial inventories are very low,” said Brew. “When there is any kind of outage, everyone starts to scramble.”
Refiners, incentivized by the ability to make incredible profits due to the shortage, are producing as much fuel as possible even though normally this is the time of year operations slow for routine repairs.
“Refiners have been running flat-out for months. If you own a refinery, you are printing money. Some are skipping maintenance because there is money to be made right now,” said Brew. “But if you run refiners for months on end, they will break down.”
Once the Exxon refinery returns to normal, gas prices should come back down. However, that relief will likely be offset by the fact that oil prices have surged to seven-month highs as traders brace for the risk of a return to all-out war in the Middle East after the election.
De Haan said Trump is “pulling every small lever he can” to cushion the blow from high prices.
“Unfortunately, they’re not adding up to much,” he said. “Until the biggest lever — diplomacy — is pulled, he’s going to continue to fight against very elevated gas and record diesel. It’s fairly ominous.”

articles.title_orig: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing
ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines said Thursday its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing.
The restrictions have raised concerns over potential revenue losses and disruptions to Mongolia’s massive mineral sector.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC, which operates Oyu Tolgoi, one of the world’s largest copper mines, said the number of truck convoys transporting copper concentrate across the Chinese border has fallen from the usual 12 to 13 per day to just around four. The restrictions affect vehicles crossing at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port, which is adjacent to Mongolia’s Gashuunsukhait Border Port.
The export cuts amount to a decline of about $300 million compared to normal operating conditions and could reach $1.2 billion if restrictions continue through the end of the year, local media reported on Wednesday.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC did not confirm the reported losses in a statement to The Associated Press on Thursday.
Mongolia is a major supplier of coal and copper to China, the world’s largest consumer of both commodities.
Mongolian border officials said the slowdown was related to infrastructure and technology upgrades at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port.
Authorities in China’s Inner Mongolia region did not immediately answer questions from the AP.
In August, Chinese authorities introduced an in-vehicle facial recognition system for truck drivers crossing the border, and installation and maintenance work have affected border processing capacity, according to the Mongolian border authorities.
Mongolia’s government said the Chinese embassy in Ulaanbaatar informed it that the work, originally due to end by late September according to Mongolian news reports, may continue until the end of December.
Mongolian Finance Minister Mendsaikhan Zagdjav said some ministers were instructed during a Cabinet meeting to visit the border crossing and meet with Chinese authorities, according to local news reports.
All transport routes on the Mongolian side remain open and the government was not aware of any political reasons behind the restrictions, said the minister of Road and Transport, Delgersaikhan Borkhuu.
Mongolia’s copper sector has become an increasingly important contributor to national export revenues. During the first nine months of 2026, copper concentrate exports reportedly reached 2 million tons.
The border crossing restrictions have also affected Mongolia’s coal exports through Gashuunsukhait, with the number of vehicles crossing falling to just over 1,000 a day from 1,300 a day, border authorities said.
Mongolia has abundant mineral resources, including coal, copper, gold, uranium and fluorspar, and its economy relies heavily on mining, which accounts for roughly a quarter of its GDP. It is particularly sensitive to disruptions to cross-border trade and fluctuations in commodity prices.
Last year, coal and copper concentrates together accounted for 82.3% of Mongolia’s merchandise exports, while 89.4% of total exports went to China. Mongolia was also China’s leading supplier of imported coking coal, accounting for approximately 51% of Chinese coking coal imports in 2025.

articles.title_orig: At least 13 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.title_zh: At least 13 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.content_orig:
At least 13 people have been killed after a Russian drone hit a busy platform at the main train station in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, officials said.
State rail company Ukrzaliznytsia said on Thursday that a jet-powered drone hit the platform where a train was preparing to leave for the nearby city of Zaporizhzhia.
Regional Governor, Oleksandr Hanzha, said on Telegram that at least 14 others were injured and six were in critical condition, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced the attack as “horrific”.
“Just how many terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and the Russian energy sector, rather than de-escalating?,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
Russia also attacked Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, damaging an educational institution, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.
Ukrainian authorities also reported overnight Russian strikes in multiple areas, including an attack in the Rivne region that killed one man.
Russian news agencies, citing the Ministry of Defence, reported that its forces struck a cargo vessel used by the Ukrainian military in the Black Sea.
Meanwhile, Russia downed most of the 613 drones launched towards Moscow overnight, in a major attack on the Russian capital, state news agency TASS reported.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that air defence forces destroyed 231 of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) on approach to the city, with the remainder neutralised on distant approaches between Wednesday evening and Thursday morning.
The Kremlin condemned the attacks on Moscow as the city hosts more than 22 African leaders at a summit, TASS reported.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was “very strange” for Kyiv to target Moscow during this time.
The Russian Defence Ministry said its air defence intercepted and destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight across regions.
Debris from downed drones also caused minor damage after falling onto the territory of an unnamed industrial facility in Sterlitamak, the second-largest city in Russia’s Bashkortostan region, Mayor Emil Shaimardanov said on Telegram.
He said the plant was operating as usual and that local air defence forces had shot down all eight Ukrainian drones involved in the attack.
The attack marks the latest in a series of major drone assaults targeting the Moscow region, following a record attack in September during which air defence forces reported shooting down more than 1,600 drones.
Both sides have reported an increase in attacks in recent months, while Moscow and Kyiv also prepare to resume peace talks next month with US mediation.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian delegation has headed to the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky, where a localised ceasefire is under way to provide humanitarian aid to the remaining residents.
The Kremlin also said it hopes aid will reach Oleshky on Thursday or Friday and that those wanting to leave the town were able to do so, Russia’s Interfax news agency reported.
So far, neither Ukraine nor Russia has reported any violations of the six-day ceasefire, which took effect early Tuesday.

Here are the main headlines from and about Germany on Thursday, October 29, 2026:
Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Thursday called on China to reduce economic imbalances between the two countries, as well as between China and Europe.
Steinmeier, who was speaking at the renowned Peking University, also urged China to work with Germany and other European nations to strengthen the international, rules-based order and "to advocate for peace and free global trade."
The German president, who holds a largely ceremonial role, spoke of his respect for China's rapid development in its economy, technology and politics, calling China a "defining world power."
But Steinmeier added, "With greatness and power comes great responsibility."
"We are not concerned about China's rise. We are watching how China rises," he said.
"We do not want to decouple from China; on the contrary, we want to structure trade in such a way that it continues to benefit both sides." This, he said, requires fair and uniform rules.
Steinmeier was referring to the high barriers European companies face when trying to operate in the Chinese market. Since China heavily subsidizes its exports to Europe, the European market comes under pressure too quickly.
This poses "the danger of one-sided vulnerability," Steinmeier said. Europeans cannot want this for their economy, just as "China does not want it for its economy."
He also called on China to exert more influence on Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.
According to Steinmeier, China's interests are also at stake in this war, just as they are in the Middle East. As a major trading power, China also needs free sea lanes, intact supply chains, and a secure energy supply.
"The longer these conflicts persist, the weaker the global economy as a whole becomes — and with it, one of its largest economies: China," the president said.
Steinmeier addressed future issues in which China should take a particular interest: climate change and artificial intelligence. He appealed to his hosts, saying that when it comes to AI, "we should jointly establish international guidelines so that the technology remains under human control," he said.
On the final day of his state visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership and hold talks with, among others, President Xi Jinping.
Steinmeier is making his first visit to China in eight years, as he seeks to boost bilateral ties.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday said North Korea was threatening "freedom throughout Europe" by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine .
After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Merz highlighted that Russia was supplying weapons to North Korea.
The chancellor said this arrangement therefore shows how "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects Korea's security."
North Korea has boosted its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pyongyang has provided Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. It has also, according to South Korean intelligence services, sent about 15,000 soldiers to fight alongside Russian forces.
In exchange, Russia provides financial backing, military technology and security guarantees to North Korea.
Before Merz's arrival on Thursday, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, according to the South Korean military.
At the start of his visit, Merz said he hoped that Korea would eventually be unified. The peninsula has been split along the 38th parallel since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953.
Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen their two nations' strategic and security ties, which includes joint military exercises and exchange of intelligence.
The chancellor is expected to conclude his trip to South Korea with a visit to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.
