Germany is looking for new partners in Asia . As Chancellor Friedrich Merz travels to Singapore, Japan and South Korea, Berlin is trying to reduce its economic dependence on China while adapting to a changing global order. But can countries in the Indo-Pacific, besides China, help Germany diversify its trade and security partnerships?
This week on Berlin Briefing, DW's Giulia Saudelli speaks with DW Business Reporter Steven Beardsley and DW Chief Political Correspondent Nina Haase, who is traveling with the chancellor.
They discuss Germany's push to "de-risk" from China, growing security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, and whether middle powers can work together to shape the future global order.
Germany and South Korea on Thursday pledged to work together on the economy, energy and security and high-tech industries, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said.
The South Korean leader made the announcement after a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Seoul.
At a joint press conference, Lee told reporters that he had asked Merz for Germany's backing in securing favorable treatment for South Korea as part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act .
The two leaders also agreed ​to ⁠improve bilateral ties to ⁠an "enhanced ​strategic partnership," Lee said.
An eight-year-old girl sustained serious injuries after she was attacked by at least one wolf at a wildlife park in Brandenburg in east Germany.
The child was brought to hospital by a rescue helicopter on Wednesday.
Local officials said a zookeeper had helped prevent other children from being attacked.
Police are investigating how and why the attack occurred, which took place during a special program for children.
Police on Thursday said their investigation was centered on a staff member who was in the enclosure with the children, a spokeswoman said.
The Teltow-Fläming district administration said the incident happened before the wildlife park's regular opening hours as part of an "Animal Keeper Day" for children.
The administration also said the attack had taken place in the polar wolf enclosure.
"While the animals in the wildlife enclosure were being watered, the wolves kept there attacked a girl and seriously injured her," the district administration said.
The zookeeper's quick action prevented "further harm to two other girls" who were also at the scene, the district added.
The park will remain closed for the time being, officials said, as authorities launch a safety review at the wildlife park, which is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin.
Police are still probing the circumstances that led to the children being inside the enclosure.
The Johannismühle Wildlife Park said it was cooperating with authorities but could not provide further details due to the open investigation.
"We deeply regret the incident, and the affected family has our full support," the park said.
The wildlife park was closed until further notice "due to technical reasons," a sign at the entrance said on Thursday.
A wolf bit a woman in a busy shopping area in Hamburg this year , in what is thought to be the first such attack since wolves were reintroduced to the country in 1998.

articles.title_orig: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.title_zh: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.content_orig:
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Analysts believe one reason for the increased empahsis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

articles.title_orig: Christine Lagarde departs at a moment of peril
articles.title_zh: Christine Lagarde departs at a moment of peril
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Marc Jones and Stella Qiu
LONDON/SYDNEY, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Europe's government bond and stock markets rallied on Thursday as traders waited on the European Central Bank's next move and for results from Amazon and Intel after Alphabet's shares became the latest to be hammered by AI spending worries.
Europe's STOXX 600 was up 0.5% despite a 1% slide in ‌Nasdaq futures and some erratic trading in Asia after Alphabet's hefty cash burn looked set to wipe nearly $400 billion off its shares later.
Both the euro and euro zone government bond market ‌yields were edging lower, meanwhile, as oil and natural gas prices dipped ahead of what is widely expected to be a pause in the ECB's rate hike cycle in Frankfurt later.
There was also breaking news that ECB President Christine Lagarde had confirmed, ​after months of speculation, that she was to step down early and leave her post in February.
Wednesday had also seen a rally in US Treasuries after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh struck a more confident tone on the inflation outlook following the Fed's decision to keep rates steady.
RBC's European Macro Strategist George Moran said his bank expects the ECB to hold rates at 2.50%, with a further final hike to 2.75% in December, although money markets are pricing as many as three additional increases.
"Widening sovereign spreads — particularly for France — give the ECB cover to avoid further aggressive tightening," Moran said, despite the recent surge in energy prices.
The main gauge of French concerns — ‌the yield gap between Paris' government bonds and triple-A-rated German Bunds — was ⁠at 153.50 basis points on Thursday, having hit a near 15-year high of almost 178 basis points last week.
Lagarde's February departure from the ECB meanwhile means French President Emmanuel Macron and other European Union leaders will be able to fill one of the bloc's most powerful economic positions before France's presidential elections in the ⁠spring.
It is a vote that opinion polls point to far-right candidate Marine Le Pen winning.
"This is driven, I would presume, by the French election," SEB Investment Management's head of asset allocation, Carl Hammer, said. "Clearly politics is having an increasingly important role for central banks."
Overnight, MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dropped nearly 0.5%, while Japan's Nikkei ended up more than 1% after another day of swings. [.T]
The region's bigger test had come from earnings. Samsung ​reported ​another set of record results thanks to booming demand for its memory chips, but it was silent on plans ​to boost returns, which sent its shares down 4%.
That weighed on South Korea's KOSPI index, ‌which fell 1.2% after a nearly 7% surge a day earlier. Another AI darling, SK Hynix, continued to surge though as its plans to return about $75 billion to shareholders this year took its two-day gain past 15%.
Nasdaq futures were pointing to a fall for US markets later. [.N]
Alphabet was down 10.5% in premarket trading after the company reported disappointing results in the firm's core search business and a massive acceleration in cash burn as it poured resources into building out AI.
That focus on AI spending will continue on Thursday too with both Intel and Amazon due to report their earnings after US markets close.
SEB's Hammer added that rising costs of developing AI were making the outlook "definitely more challenging" for asset allocators following the years-long stock market bull run.
"We are keeping a constructive view as of now (on equities) but it's getting more complicated ... ‌the bulk of the risks in portfolios are driven by the AI infrastructure cycle."
Macro data is set to keep ​coming too, with both US personal consumption expenditures figures — the Fed's preferred gauge of inflation — and US Q3 GDP data ​due to be released later.
Forecasts are centred on a 0.3% monthly rise in the core measure ​of PCE inflation, picking up from a 0.2% gain the previous month.
Markets are still 80% priced for a rate rise in December despite Wednesday's dovish comments from ‌Warsh, which led to a steepening of the Treasury yield curve. The 2-year Treasury ​yield fell about 5 basis points overnight and was ​last at 4.68%.
The dollar was flat against its major peers after a 0.2% dip on Wednesday following the Fed decision.
Ahead of the ECB, the euro was hovering around $1.1145, having fallen almost 2% this month against the dollar and 2.5% against sterling. [GVD/EUR]
Data also show investors have built up their biggest short position on the euro in a decade, one that is currently worth almost $19 ​billion.
In the commodity markets, Brent futures fell 1% to $114 a barrel after the ‌Wall Street Journal reported US Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei in an effort to revive peace negotiations.
Qatari mediators have ​also presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war, an official briefed on the negotiations told Reuters, though a senior Iranian official dismissed what had been ​presented as unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.
(Reporting by Marc Jones; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

articles.title_orig: Protests erupt in Spain after train crash kills dozens
articles.title_zh: Protests erupt in Spain after train crash kills dozens
articles.content_orig:
URDA, Spain — Spain began three days of mourning Thursday after at least 69 people were killed and dozens more injured in the country’s deadliest train crash in decades . But anger is mounting about the alleged incompetence that allowed the accident to happen and protesters clashed with police overnight outside the country’s transport ministry.
Once considered one of the country’s crowning achievements, Spain’s high-speed rail network had not endured a deadly crash since it came into service over 30 years ago.
After the second train accident in less than a year , the tragedy has deepened the feeling among many that there is something broken in Spanish society.  The crash follows weeks of protests.
Rising costs and a housing shortage that is pricing many Spaniards out of the housing market, have already triggered massive and sometimes deadly protests across the country, and piled the pressure on the Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
On Wednesday, four weeks before the country goes to the polls in a national election, Sanchez visited the site in the central province of Toledo where a quiet stretch of rail lined by olive groves had been turned into a scene of devastation.
Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off. Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident in the countryside in the province of Toledo after one train crashed into another that was stationary on the line.
Hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police, firefighters and soldiers attended the scene to rescue survivors and recover bodies, before cranes were brought in to move parts of the damaged trains late Wednesday.
Several Americans were hurt, according to the State Department, which did not provide further details.
Jacksonville firefighter Josue Garcia-Otero was on board with seven of his family members.
“We got to safety first, then began treating other patients that were critically injured,” Garcia-Otero said in a news release issued by the Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department.  “My wife is a nurse, and she was helping too.”
Pledging an investigation and improvements to prevent a similar tragedy in future, Sánchez said it was clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail.”
It was “not acceptable  for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year,” he said, referring to an incident in January when 46 people died after one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in the south of the country.
Both crashes involved trains operated by the state-owned RENFE company and the privately owned IRYO.
His transport minister, Óscar Puente, said that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command center for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed.
Puente, who is facing calls to resign, said the train engineers were not to blame, but instead a security system had stopped working because of a computer malfunction, causing all trains on the line to stop at about 8:30 a.m. local time (5:30 a.m. ET).
Shortly afterwards he said central command had told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, adding that never should have happened and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Riot police used tear gas outside his transport ministry in Madrid late Wednesday after far-right protesters gathered outside and pushed against a cordon set up by officers. Some threw flares and other objects as some chanted slogans against Puente and Sánchez.
Quite what effect the accident will have on Sánchez’s political ambitions remains unclear. The prime minister called a snap election next month after his Socialist party suffered several defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country’s housing crisis.
His minority government had put forward two decree laws aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market after nationwide protests following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid apartment . Maricarmen Abascal, who was a wheelchair user, was eventually allowed to return but died in hospital before she could do so.
Sánchez who took power in 2018 has weathered several crises during his premiership including the Covid-19 pandemic and the global inflation rise.
But he has faced attacks from right-wing parties over his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both deny, and polls show he is facing and uphill battle to win votes ahead of the election next month.
Raf Sanchez is a foreign correspondent for NBC News.
Michael Fiorentino is a London-based producer for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
articles.title_zh: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
articles.content_orig:
Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson is set to have his work presented in two weeks’ time at one of the most prestigious conferences in theoretical computer science. As of Monday, much of that work is “dead,” he says, after AI showed that a 27-year-old hypothesis underpinning it is wrong.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic claimed this week to have disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH). Vast swaths of theoretical computer science research on complexity and algorithm design have been built on the premise that the effort it takes to solve certain problems increases exponentially with the size of the problem.
Jonsson expects his predicament will be “very common” at the IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, where his work will be presented by one of his coauthors. “People will start the talks: ‘ETH is false, half of my paper does not work,’” he says. It’s a vexing problem, Jonsson says, “but at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.”
Researchers haven’t independently verified, let alone had time to fully understand, the AI-produced proofs, which both firms have published on GitHub in both natural language and its machine-checkable Lean format. OpenAI has asked the UC Santa Barbara computer scientists who originally proposed the hypothesis, plus an MIT academic who has refuted a version of ETH, to rally researchers to unpack the proofs. So far, this effort includes a Google form asking for volunteers and feedback, and a commitment from OpenAI to fund a conference on the topic.
UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov plans to join the effort, as he estimates the result—if confirmed—will render him “galactically wrong” and make around 50 of his published papers either “pointless” or in need of a revisit.
“It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.”
Thore Husfeldt, head of the algorithms research group at the IT University of Copenhagen, had spent most of this year thinking about one single problem in his subfield. “As far as I can tell, it’s now all irrelevant,” he tells WIRED. Having first formulated a version of the hypothesis now disproved by OpenAI, he has been writing calculations on his blackboard to figure out what other parts of his work might have become obsolete due to the “once-in-a-generation result.” Unlike the ennui that has gripped math researchers who have faced similarly field-upending proofs generated by AI models, though, Husfeldt expressed enthusiasm about the new results.
The finding is “fantastic,” he says. “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room,” he explains. “It's like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.”
For centuries, science has advanced through making hypotheses and proving them wrong. It also isn’t unusual for an academic to be scooped or have their work otherwise undercut by another research group. But AI has accelerated this, obliterating whole research programs and spooking researchers in specific fields of math and science who wonder where they stand now that machines can outperform them.
“The last few months have been really tough. It's a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people,” Husfeldt says. “That is psychologically taxing for many people,” he says, adding that his department has considered hiring an occupational psychologist because “some people are really depressed and really sad.”
Researchers have also been overwhelmed by the volume of content now being produced, thanks to AI, including slop-level results. Midway through the interview, Husfeldt receives what he suspects to be an AI-generated 17-page paper on the consequences of the ETH result from a random Gmail account. He won’t read it: “Reading math is a very big investment of cognitive time,” he says.
OpenAI has directly contributed to this; earlier this month, it dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub, to the annoyance of academics , who complain this makes it difficult to digest the results. Adding to the frustration were several documents that contained errors, reflecting what some mathematicians saw as a hasty rollout designed to juice the company’s planned initial public offering rather than moving the field forward. This time around, OpenAI’s 60-odd-page paper on ETH seems to be written better than the companies’ past publications, academics tell WIRED.
They are now scrambling to unpack the paper and find what other results they can quickly deduce from it.
If ETH is false and it doesn’t, in fact, take exponentially more time to solve problems as they become more complex, that’s “exciting,” says Victor Lagerkvist, an associate professor at Linköping. He plans to return to problems he had previously given up on under the assumption ETH was accurate.
OpenAI’s finding could also have impacts on the cryptography that underpins web security, which is based on the assumption that certain mathematical problems take an impractically long time to solve. While this particular result doesn’t directly affect cryptography, “it should definitely scare some cryptosystem designers,” says Lokshtanov.
That’s why continued human and AI-assisted work in theoretical computer science is important, Husfeldt adds: “We want the open scientific process to identify our misunderstandings about computation, in particular because lots of modern digital infrastructure is built on assumptions about computation.”
As for Linköping’s Jonsson, he plans to revisit both his own and others’ papers that hinge on ETH being true, and believes his conference paper may eventually be salvageable through another method. He’s excited to look into the details of OpenAI’s proof and see what he can learn from it and apply it to new problems. Even though it undoes the assumptions underpinning his work, having a verdict for ETH is something he could only “dream of” before, he says. “These are exciting times,” he adds. “Most people would never experience anything like this in their career.”
“I don’t care if it's a human-written proof, or it's written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.’’

articles.title_orig: How Netanyahu Used Fear, Again, to Win More Votes Than Anyone Else
articles.title_zh: How Netanyahu Used Fear, Again, to Win More Votes Than Anyone Else
articles.content_orig:
In a political career that has spanned more than three decades, Benjamin Netanyahu has been written off too many times to count, only to prove the obituaries were penned prematurely. Israel’s election results this week appear to give the prime minister’s opponents a chance to end his run, but in the country’s ruthless political system, it’s no guarantee.
By Wednesday night, most votes had been counted. But there is no clear winner for Israel’s top post, setting up weeks — possibly months — in which Netanyahu’s political survival remains on the line.
With the vote counting nearing its conclusion, Netanyahu’s Likud party remains the largest party in the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, with an estimated 26 seats. But his right-wing bloc has lost its majority, set to win only 53 seats, short of the 61-seat majority needed to govern.
Netanyahu hasn’t won. But he hasn’t lost, either — at least not yet. Now, he has to stop his rivals from building their own government, and he may survive again.
On paper, the opposition holds roughly 67 seats, but that arithmetic is fractured by ideological, national and personal rivalries. Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot , won 21 seats, but the Jewish opposition parties total only 48, well short of victory. To reach 61, they would need the support of two Arab parties, Raam and the Joint List, which are projected to win a record 19 seats between them. Analysts say that record turnout by Arabs or Palestinian citizens of Israel was in part a backlash to four years of a far-right national security minister under whom crime in the Arab community soared, and members of the community have blamed the trend on negligent policing. They have also been affected by a rise in racism following October 7 and Israel’s war in Gaza — and have been highly critical of settler violence, all factors that could have mobilized them to vote.
This is where the math gets complicated. Raam is an Islamist party that draws heavily from Israel’s Bedouin community. Its leader, Mansour Abbas, became the first Arab politician to join an Israeli government following the country’s 2021 election. The Joint List, projected to be the bigger Arab party, combines several smaller parties: the Communist Hadash, secularist Taal and nationalist Balad factions.
On Wednesday, Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, called on his partners to count the Arab parties as part of the bloc, rejecting what he called Netanyahu’s “racist division between Jewish and Arab votes.” But two of Eisenkot’s right-wing allies, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman, have opposed any government that depends on the Arab parties. (They have not issued a statement on the issue since polls closed.)
The Joint List said Wednesday that it was ready for political cooperation and willing to do “do everything in its power to bring Netanyahu’s rule to an end.”
A source close to Netanyahu said his main post-election goal is to delegitimize and therefore prevent the Jewish-Arab political cooperation that could send him home.
“He is very concerned about a minority government,” the source said. Netanyahu even plans to pressure individual opposition lawmakers not to cooperate with the Arab parties. After campaigning against them throughout the election, Likud issued a statement Wednesday accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the election” through bribery, threats, violence and forgery, echoing election fraud claims from his closest ally, US President Donald Trump. The Central Elections Committee said Wednesday it was examining the complaint, but the committee had already dismissed thousands of complaints from the different parties on election day.
Netanyahu plans to “neutralize this possibility by all means,” the source told CNN, “including launching an attack on Iran or enlisting President Trump to intervene in Israeli politics on his behalf.”
The opposition fears that Netanyahu could use a security crisis to stall or block a new government. Before the election, Netanyahu had pressed Trump to launch a joint attack on Iran, but Washington held off, partly because Israeli military chief of staff Eyal Zamir warned it could disrupt the vote. An Israeli security source told CNN the operational plans are ready and awaiting Trump’s approval, possibly after the US midterms.
“There is no way to know what Netanyahu will do,” an opposition source told CNN. “We are aware that he may try to push for another escalation.” Another source said that Netanyahu “will do everything he can not to leave the prime minister’s office, including domestic and external chaos.”
Eisenkot, a former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, called on Israel’s security chiefs Tuesday night to remember that “Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate and without public confidence.” Speaking to supporters shortly after exit polls were published, Eisenkot declared that the public “has chosen change.”
In his first reaction to the updated results since Tuesday night’s speech, Eisenkot said he remains committed to “bringing change to Israel.”
The numbers can still change. By Wednesday evening, the Central Elections Committee is expected to finish counting most ballots. Attention now turns to double-envelope ballots from home by soldiers, prisoners, hospital patients and staff, diplomats abroad and voters with disabilities. The committee estimates there are between 430,000 and 480,000 double envelopes, enough for over 10 seats. They are counted separately in a special verification process, with final results expected Thursday.
Then the political maneuvering begins in earnest.
The next step runs through President Isaac Herzog, whose post-election role is pivotal. His job here is to consult with all elected parties on the candidate they recommend as prime minister, before picking the one he believes is most likely to secure a 61-seat majority. This is not necessarily the leader of the largest party but the one with the most plausible path to a coalition.
Eisenkot is likely to collect more recommendations than Netanyahu, since the Arab parties are expected to back him.
Then the clock starts ticking.
The chosen candidate has 28 days — and a possible 14-day extension — to negotiate with other parties over cabinet posts, budgets and policies in order to form a government. If he fails, the mandate passes to another candidate for another four weeks. If he fails, too, the Knesset gets a short window to put forward an alternative candidate. If that fails, the country goes to automatic elections.
Netanyahu, as caretaker prime minister, has a built-in advantage. If Eisenkot receives the mandate first — and fails — all he needs to do is wait for his time to pass. And if Israel finds itself headed for new elections, Netanyahu will remain caretaker for months.
Eisenkot isn’t out of options entirely.
Even without forming a government, the opposition could still leverage its parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker and other key positions. That could limit Netanyahu’s ability to govern and even enable the opposition to advance legislation.
But Eisenkot, a retired lieutenant general, isn’t on his preferred battlefield. Netanyahu’s coalition remains incredibly loyal, and he doesn’t have to worry in any real way about defections. The same cannot be said for Eisenkot. His diverse coalition is far less ideologically aligned, and even the tiniest step could splinter the bloc and send the country back to elections.
For now, the focus is on Herzog, whose role is even more important given the current deadlock. With neither bloc holding a clear majority, he may try to push Netanyahu and Eisenkot to form a unity government.
“We must do everything to avoid another round of elections,” Herzog said Wednesday. He called on party leaders to come to consultations with an “open mind.”

articles.content_orig:
Iran's Houthi allies said Thursday that a Saudi strike on a residential area in Yemen's western Taiz province killed 12 people, as the two sides continued to exchange fire in the reignited Yemeni civil war.
"As an initial toll, 12 citizens were killed and three others were critically injured when the Saudi enemy targeted the homes of the families of Ibrahim Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz and Al-Raabi Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz in Al-Barah, Maqbana district," the Houthi health ministry said in a statement shared by the group's Saba news agency.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in Yemen in July, months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis. The Saudis, who back Yemen's government, have engaged in fighting with the Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast and in deadly back-and-forth strikes.
Iran has used some 5,000 agencies to help it slip past the U.S. naval blockade to import hardware, explosives and trucks needed for its drone and missile programs over land, sea and air, according to a report by the Reuters news agency .
The secret network of military agencies has helped Iran usher at least $2 billion in components into the country since 2025, evading Western sanctions and, since earlier this year, the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels.
Some of the agencies are linked to Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), others to business conglomerates run by the country's elite, Reuters said.
Between January 2025 and June 2026, before the U.S. blockade was imposed but with myriad U.S. and international sanctions in place, a single company, MOD 346428, imported large quantities of rocket propellants, explosives and weapons parts crucial for drones and missile production, as well as trucks that can be used as missile launchers. The hardware was brought in from China, Russia and Germany, Reuters reported.
The agencies all use the address of Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics in Tehran. Most were established in 2013, when Iran was struggling under international sanctions, the investigation found.
Iran's Intelligence Ministry said Thursday that it had dismantled four alleged terrorist cells and arrested 16 suspects in the central and southern parts of Sistan and Baluchestan Province, while detaining three more individuals accused of gathering and transmitting information about security and defense sites in the country's southeast.
In a statement, the provincial intelligence directorate said the operations were carried out in recent days following public tips and ongoing intelligence and operational surveillance, in cooperation with other provincial security forces. It alleged that the cells were affiliated with terrorist groups linked to the United States and Israel.
The ministry said some of the 16 detainees had arrived from abroad. It also alleged that several were involved in the killing of law enforcement personnel in Iranshahr. The suspects have been handed over to judicial authorities, according to the statement, carried by Iran's official IRNA news agency.
Security forces reportedly seized a cache of weapons and ammunition, including nine Kalashnikov rifles, two American-made M4 rifles and seven handguns.
In a separate operation, authorities arrested three people accused of collecting and transmitting information on the locations of military headquarters and defense and security facilities in southern Sistan and Baluchestan to networks the ministry described as linked to U.S. and Israeli intelligence and media operations.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said Thursday that its electronic warfare unit had intercepted and safely landed a U.S. reconnaissance drone west of the Strait of Hormuz, claiming the craft had been conducting surveillance of Iranian air defense systems along the Persian Gulf coastline and the strait.
"Through an offensive electronic warfare operation, the fighters of the IRGC Navy's electronic warfare unit, with the help of Almighty God, successfully managed to safely land an American terrorist army reconnaissance and deception drone of the MQM-170 type in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, after detecting and identifying it and taking control of its guidance and control systems," a statement from the IRGC navy read.
The bulletin added that the IRGC had "determined that the aircraft had taken off from the coast of one of the countries on the southern shores of the Persian Gulf."
Vice President JD Vance has sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei seeking to restart peace negotiations, according to multiple reports, but President Trump insists it is a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he is still mulling whether to resume major military operations against Iran or make a peace deal after next week's midterm elections, according to various outlets.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Vance was engaging directly with Mohsen Rezaei, one of Iran's most powerful hard-liners, in an effort to revive negotiations, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter.
Vance sent the letter to Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' longest-serving former commander, at President Trump's direction, according to The Journal. The initiative seeks to establish whether Washington and Tehran can find common ground to avert a renewed conflict, the paper reported.
According to The New York Times , the letter, sent last week via Qatari mediators and delivered to Rezaei on Sunday, proposed an early meeting between American and Iranian officials, with Vance offering to lead the U.S. negotiating team.
The Times said Rezaei was expected to issue a formal response by Thursday. The letter did not specify a date or location for negotiations, but U.S. and Iranian officials were quoted by the newspaper as saying direct talks could begin as soon as next week in Qatar or Turkey.
According to Axios , Vance's letter explicitly stated that any negotiations aimed at preventing new U.S. military strikes would require discussions on Iran's nuclear program.
Asked Wednesday about Vance's contact with Iranian officials, Mr. Trump told reporters he had not sought to renew peace talks, but "what that is, they [Iran] need help with medical supplies and various things. He [Vance] asked me what I thought and I said, 'If you want to do that that's okay.' Basically it's getting supplies in to help people who are not well."
An official briefed on the diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war.
A response is expected from Tehran by the end of the week, most likely Saturday, the official added.
On Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' said Thursday that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines while attempting to transit what it described as "the unauthorized southern route" through the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy's public relations office said the incidents occurred over the past 24 hours, adding that the vessels were subsequently stranded along the southern shores of the strait.
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a southern shipping lane through the vital waterway, which President Trump himself declared mine-free at the end of August. Iran insists vessels can only transit the strait through routes it administers closer to its coast in the north of the strait, in coordination with Iranian authorities.

articles.title_orig: FTC orders Delta, Uber and others to hand over data on algorithmic pricing
articles.title_zh: FTC orders Delta, Uber and others to hand over data on algorithmic pricing
articles.content_orig:
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson warns of online radicalization, vows to protect kids in the A.I. race and crack down on ticket bots to lower costs for families on ‘Varney & Co.’
Federal regulators announced Wednesday that they are examining whether major airlines, ride-hailing companies, delivery services and retailers are using personal data to charge different customers different prices for the same products and services or determine how much gig workers are paid.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said it launched an inquiry into nine companies, ordering them to provide information about how they use consumers' and workers' personal data to set prices and compensation.
The orders were sent to Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart , according to the FTC.
The agency said it is seeking information to assess whether prices for airline tickets , rides, food deliveries and other products or services vary from person to person.
DOLLAR GENERAL SUED BY FTC AND 20 STATES, ACCUSED OF OVERCHARGING CUSTOMERS
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said consumers deserve to know whether companies use their browsing history or other personal information to determine the highest prices they can charge. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Federal regulators will then examine whether factors such as loyalty programs and the analysis of personal data by superintelligence algorithms influence consumer pricing and worker compensation.
"We intend to scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service," FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.
" Consumers deserve to know whether companies use their web surfing habits or other personal data to estimate the highest price they can charge each consumer," Ferguson continued.
Ferguson said workers "deserve to know if their compensation is affected by how companies use their personal data."
AMERICAN AIRLINES SAYS AIRFARES COULD STAY ELEVATED EVEN IF FUEL PRICES DROP
Walmart was ordered to provide information to federal regulators about its pricing practices as part of an FTC inquiry into personalized pricing. (Sundry Photography/Getty Images / Getty Images)
In its news release announcing the inquiry, the FTC noted that ride-hailing and food-delivery companies may offer workers varying compensation based on "opaque formulas."
These companies, the FTC said, "may engage in personalized compensation based on their drivers’ personal data, such as their phone usage or acceptance history for past offers."
A spokesperson for Instacart told FOX Business that the online grocery marketplace "does not and will not engage in surveillance pricing."
"We do not use personal information to set prices, and we never will," the spokesperson said.
WALMART ROLLS OUT NEW BUNDLE COMBINING WALMART+, SAM’S CLUB PLUS
JetBlue told FOX Business that it does not use customers' personal information or browsing histories to set individual fares, saying ticket prices are based on demand and seat availability. (Mario Tama / Getty Images)
"We appreciate the FTC’s focus on this practice, we are committed to transparency and improving affordability for customers, and we will continue engaging with policymakers and regulators to ensure they understand how pricing on our platform works."
JetBlue told FOX Business that it "does not use personal information or web browsing history to set individual pricing."
"Fares are determined by demand and seat availability, and all customers have access to the same fares on jetblue.com and our mobile app," the airline added.
Delta also denied using personal data to individually price fares, saying it has never used, tested or planned to use a fare product that targets customers with individualized offers based on personal data.
FOX Business has reached out to United, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Target and Walmart for comment.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The FTC said companies that fail to provide the requested information could face legal action to compel compliance. Each company has 45 days from the date it receives the order to respond.

articles.title_orig: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.title_zh: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.content_orig:
Students gifted only water celery or white wormwood, choosing these fragrant plants to symbolise a pure pursuit of knowledge
While it is common for Chinese people to hold banquets for teachers upon graduation as a way of honouring them – a traditional value – in ancient China, students expressed their respect for teachers differently: by presenting them with vegetables.
The tradition began in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). On the first day of school, students wore blue gowns and brought their teachers wild vegetables they had gathered themselves. They then bowed reverently before memorial tablets honouring ancient sages. The ceremony was followed by a group dance, which also expressed the students’ respect for their teachers and their dedication to their studies.
Not just any vegetables could be presented to teachers on this day. Water celery and white wormwood were preferred because they were seen as clean, fragrant and ethereal, symbolising the students’ pure pursuit of knowledge.

articles.title_orig: Alphabet and Microsoft are on both sides of the AI boom's biggest bills: Chart of the Day
articles.title_zh: Alphabet and Microsoft are on both sides of the AI boom's biggest bills: Chart of the Day
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street bought Microsoft and sold Alphabet after the two reported quarterly earnings Wednesday night. Both rent computing power to the AI labs and own stakes in them, but this quarter Microsoft cashed in while Alphabet's bets cost it.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) stock rose about 2% after hours, while Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) fell over 9%, on track for its worst day since October 2023, after its sales came up short .
For Microsoft, the labs show up as sales. OpenAI paid it $10 billion in the quarter that ended in September, according to Microsoft's quarterly filing. That's about 11% of Microsoft's $92 billion in revenue, and more than its Xbox and Windows businesses brought in combined.
Some of that money is still owed. OpenAI's unpaid bills to Microsoft rose to about $7 billion from $6 billion three months earlier. Microsoft also owns about 24% of the ChatGPT maker, but the stake barely moved its profit this time.
The order book cooled, too. Microsoft's backlog — revenue customers have signed up for, but Microsoft hasn't yet booked — slipped to about $677 billion, and new bookings fell 12% from a year earlier. CFO Amy Hood blamed "large Azure commitments in the prior year" for the tough comparison.
Alphabet's bets on the labs worked the other way. Its stakes in other companies, including roughly 14% of Anthropic and a piece of SpaceX ( SPCX ), supplied about $6 of its $9.11 in per-share profit in the second quarter.
This time they cost it. A nearly $9 billion loss on those holdings cut earnings by $0.55 a share, to $2.12. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the call that the loss came "primarily" from SpaceX, whose stock dropped about 12% during the quarter.
Alphabet is also footing the bill to build. It spent $51 billion on data centers and equipment in the quarter, more than double a year earlier, and burned about $9 billion in free cash flow — the cash left after those investments — for a second straight quarter. Microsoft generated about $19 billion and said it expects to stay positive this fiscal year.
To cover the gap, Alphabet bought back no stock, sold about $29 billion of bonds and $12 billion of new shares, and nearly tripled its long-term debt this year to about $125 billion. Meta ( META ) took a similar route with its nearly $100 billion stock sale .
The payoff is showing up in Google Cloud, where revenue doubled to about $31 billion and the backlog of signed contracts rose to $561 billion from $514 billion three months earlier. Anthropic has committed at least $115 billion to Google for computing power, according to its IPO filing, about a fifth of that backlog by Yahoo Finance calculations.
The next swing could come from Anthropic itself. Its IPO could start trading as soon as Nov. 16 , and once it does, Alphabet's stake gets valued at the market price each quarter. At the reported $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation, that could turn the drag back into a windfall by year-end.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella doesn't want to lean on the labs forever. Asked on the call where Azure's AI growth is coming from, he said he's after breadth, not "four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you and you can show a few quarters of growth."
"That's not a business as far as I'm concerned," he said.

articles.title_orig: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.title_zh: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.content_orig:
A US cruise ship MV. Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville southern Cambodia, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
A couple passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, stands for an interview with his wife, Lynn Motoya, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX stock slides back toward $140 as smaller space names leave it behind
articles.title_zh: SpaceX stock slides back toward $140 as smaller space names leave it behind
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX took its worst one-day hit last Thursday since early August, when its biggest share unlock yet freed up to 1.3 billion shares to trade. Roughly a week later, it's back at the same floor, and the rest of the space trade has left it behind.
SpaceX ( SPCX ) shares slipped again on Thursday during premarket trading, along with nearly every space stock.
$140 has been SpaceX's floor since the summer. It marked the top of the stock's August trading range before a breakout, and it sits about halfway between the August low near $108 and the $172 ceiling that capped rallies in June and October.
That makes $140 support , a price where buyers have repeatedly stepped in. They did it twice this month, and the stock is back there again.
SpaceX fell about 9% on Oct. 22 as those shares unlocked.
Since then, the smaller names have done the running. Rocket Lab ( RKLB ), Firefly Aerospace ( FLY ), Intuitive Machines ( LUNR ) and AST SpaceMobile ( ASTS ) gained roughly 8% to 14% from the Oct. 22 close through Tuesday, while SpaceX barely budged.
That bounce followed a much rougher month for the group: over the past 30 days, those four are down roughly 20% to 35%, compared with a loss of about 3% for SpaceX.
The pullback comes as investors gear up for Anthropic's IPO, the next mega-listing, with JPMorgan again set to lead retail share sales as it did for SpaceX. SpaceX sits about a third below its June record close near $212.
A sustained break below $140 would open the door to a deeper slide toward the August low near $108. To turn the chart around, bulls first need to get back above the 50-day moving average, near $150, before taking another run at $172.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) report after the bell. How much more they plan to spend building AI data centers is the number most likely to move a stock that's now mostly an AI company .

articles.title_orig: Putin praises Elon Musk as a ‘genius’ as Russia develops Starlink alternative
articles.title_zh: Putin praises Elon Musk as a ‘genius’ as Russia develops Starlink alternative
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk a "genius," as he revealed the two are in "close contact" about developing a Russian alternative to Starlink.
"Elon Musk is a genius, truly a genius," Putin said at the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on Wednesday. "He has already had more than 5,000 such satellites in orbit, while we are only taking the first steps," he said at an event where he discussed Russia's own satellite connectivity project, Rassvet.
Rassvet is a satellite internet constellation in low Earth orbit, built by the Russian private aerospace company Bureau 1440. It has 31 satellites in orbit currently, out of 32 launched since March of this year, according to satellite tracker Orbital Radar. Twenty-six are in their working orbit at about 509 kilometers.
"We are proud that we have begun doing this and that we have started doing it independently," Putin said according to a translation. "We are in close contact with our U.S. partners, including Mr Musk."
"In orbit, it is very important not to interfere with one another and to adhere to certain rules, discipline, and order. Both we and our U.S. partners value this mutual understanding. Together with Mr. Musk, despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely."
SpaceX, Starlink's owner, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.
Starlink operates a constellation of more than 11,000 satellites in orbit , providing high-speed internet access to 174 countries, according to the company.
The service drew attention earlier this month after Ukraine accused SpaceX and Musk of imposing restrictions that slowed the country's military satellite internet access, thereby harming its defensive capabilities.
The restrictions affected Starshield, SpaceX’s satellite communications service for governments, causing drones and other moving terminals to lose or experience degraded connectivity above roughly 100 miles per hour, according to Ukrainian officials.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed the restricted service for disrupting its air defense capabilities during frequent Russian air attacks.
Musk has said Starshield is controlled by the U.S. government, and ultimately the president, while other reports have said the restriction was imposed by Musk. U.S. President Donald Trump has denied ordering the restriction.
The White House and SpaceX did not respond to CNBC requests for comment on whether the service had been limited and where such an order came from.
Musk later said Ukraine had breached Starlink's terms of service by using a civilian commercial network for offensive drone strikes. Ukraine has denied doing so.
Putin's remarks late Wednesday come amid continued strikes between Russia and Ukraine as the war closes in on five years.
Early Thursday, 13 people were killed and 10 injured in a Russian jet-powered drone attack on a railway station in Dnipro in eastern Ukraine, according to regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha .
Russia also ​attacked Ukraine's second-biggest city, Kharkiv, damaging an ​educational ​institution, the city's ⁠Mayor Ihor ​Terekhov wrote ​on ⁠Telegram, while Russia's Ministry of Defense said it intercepted and destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles overnight.
U.S.-brokered peace talks between Putin, Zelenskyy and Trump may happen next month.
Zelenskyy said on ​Wednesday that preparations are underway for a trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi, to take place by Nov. 10.
Moscow has not yet ​proposed a specific date for the talks, which will depend on several factors, including the Iran war, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri ‌Ushakov was quoted saying on Wednesday.
"It will also depend on the situation ​on the battlefield and the situation in general. You can see the situation now ​in the Middle East. It just doesn't allow us to hold it in the near future. That's my assumption," Ushakov told journalists, Reuters reported, citing Russian media.
- CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
articles.title_zh: How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
A drone operator with the military call sign Professor operates a Lupynis-10-TFL-1 from The Fourth Law at a test site in central Ukraine. Paula Bronstein/for NPR hide caption
KYIV, Ukraine — Like many tech entrepreneurs in Ukraine, Yaroslav Azhnyuk turned to developing drone warfare after Russia's 2022 invasion.
Drones have transformed the way wars are fought. Azhnyuk says artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable.
"When the other side has orders of magnitudes higher capabilities, it gives you an asymmetric advantage," he says. "It can make you 10,000 times more effective."
Azhnyuk runs the Ukraine-based defense firms The Fourth Law and Odd Systems. They are among the top companies producing AI-powered drones in Ukraine. Dozens of Ukrainian military units already use their autonomous drone, called the Lupynis-10-TFL-1.
Russia is also deploying AI-enabled drones against Ukraine. AI warfare is part of a high-tech arms race that has many worried, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.
Azhnyuk told NPR that he acknowledges the concern over destructive weapons but says it's not specific to AI.
"It has been with humanity since the invention of fire or steel," he says. "Any kind of tool can be used for good or for bad. And in the end, it's the human that decides how to use that tool."
Cameras that "fling explosives"
Azhnyuk is 37, a gregarious computer scientist who hails from a family of scholars and scientists. NPR meets him in a conference room in Kyiv; for security reasons he asked us not to reveal much else about the location.
He worked for years in Silicon Valley and started several companies, including Petcube , which makes smartphone-powered cameras that use artificial intelligence to watch and even entertain pets while they're alone.
"These cameras allow pet parents to watch pets when they're not at home," he says, "and fling treats to them and shine a laser toy for them. We sold a million of these devices that are quite popular in the U.S."
After Russia launched its full-scale war, Azhnyuk, by then living in Ukraine, pivoted to the defense space.
"I was like, OK, I've got to move on from Petcube and do something to protect my country," he says. "And so now we're making not cameras that fling treats but cameras that fling explosives at people who came to occupy our land."
The cameras he's talking about are part of an image recognition system incorporated into first-person-view or FPV drones.
"We are leaders in autonomous drones and thermal cameras," he says.
A Lupynis-10-TFL-1 drone is seen in the air at a test site in central Ukraine. Paula Bronstein for NPR hide caption
A drone named after a poet
The autonomous Lupynis TFL-1 drone combines a small, affordable FPV drone with an autonomous terminal guidance unit. That means the drone has an onboard computer and AI technology that takes control during the last 500 meters (or 0.3 miles) of the flight.
"But it's very different from, say, the kind of AI that sits on those data centers that power Claude," he says. "Or even the kind of AI that does self-driving for your Tesla."
Azhnyuk says this AI technology uses simple tools to recognize images and make smart software "which then allows you either to navigate autonomously without a human or to choose a target autonomously or to fly toward the target autonomously."
The Fourth Law's autonomous drone is named after the 20th century Ukrainian poet and political activist Anatoliy Lupynis, who endured decades of Soviet imprisonment and psychiatric torture. The company named all its weapons after Ukrainian intellectuals and artists killed or persecuted by Russians in the last century.
"It is important for us to help to resurrect those people," Azhnyuk says. "Their ideas are still with us. And now they're fighting back."
"The drone is doing everything itself"
The Fourth Law teams test the Lupynis TFL-1 drones every day. We meet one team in an overgrown field outside Kyiv. They've set up a fold-out table near a copse of trees and a hornets' nest.
A slight, sandy-haired man stands up from the fold-out table and says he's the head of the test and integration team. He uses the military call sign Stab. The Fourth Law asked NPR not to reveal this location or the identities of those who work here for security reasons.
"So you see here is our camera, plus the microcomputer inside this 3-D model," Stab says. "All of the mind is here," he adds with a laugh.
The microcomputer inside the drone runs on a deep-learning neural network that uses hours of combat footage to recognize targets.
"Like vehicles, light-armored vehicles, tanks, and flying objects," he says.
The drone begins its flight guided by a pilot, who also asked us to use his call sign, Professor. He navigates the drone with a control stick. He selects a target and checks a video monitor. Then he sees a red flash.
"That means it has locked," Stab says.
The drone has locked onto its target: a dilapidated car an employee is driving along a dirt road. Professor lets go of the control stick. The drone flies itself to the car. The microcomputer inside constantly runs algorithms to keep it on course.
"See, Professor is doing nothing, and the drone is doing everything itself," Stab says.
On the battlefield, the drone would carry an explosive to hit the car. The test drone doesn't have one.
Stab says AI drones are useful because they're hard to jam. He also insists safeguards are in place so The Fourth Law drones won't go rogue. Humans select the target, he says.
Yaroslav Azhnyuk, the founder of the AI drone company The Fourth Law, previously worked in Silicon Valley and started several companies, including one that makes smartphone-powered cameras that use artificial intelligence to watch and entertain pets while they're alone. Paula Bronstein/for NPR hide caption
Survival vs. the ethics of AI
Back in the conference room, Azhnyuk says his company's AI-powered drones are not killer robots.
"They're very far from a Terminator kind of scenario, right?" he says. "These are just sort of calculators. Like they're no more likely for a Terminator uprising than a warehouse with artillery shells."
He does acknowledge, though, that AI is developing quickly. "It's not unthinkable," he says, "to imagine that some years in the future there will be drones that will be able to make their own decisions on designating targets or not."
That's the future. Right now he is focused on what Ukraine needs today.
"Our adversaries are using the very same technologies, and if they use AI for decision-making in an offensive scenario, and if we refuse to use AI in decision-making in a defensive scenario, we've lost, right?" he says. "Because their systems are capable of making decisions in microseconds, and human control takes minutes, hours and sometimes days."
If Ukraine loses, he says, "there's no way for us to argue about the ethics of AI."
The most important thing, he says, is don't die.
NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this story from Kyiv.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Chief Seen as Target of Chinese Spy Plot
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Chief Seen as Target of Chinese Spy Plot
articles.content_orig:
A Chinese executive suspected of helping Beijing obtain restricted American artificial intelligence chips also developed a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, raising concerns that China could gain sensitive information through her access to the technology leader.
U.S. intelligence agencies concluded that the executive, Alice Huang, was gathering information for Beijing, The New York Times reported on Thursday.
President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings roughly a year ago but chose not to act, according to people familiar with the classified intelligence.
The discovery brought together two concerns for Washington: China's efforts to acquire advanced American chips and its potential access to the head of the company producing them.
Nvidia's chips power sophisticated AI systems, making the company central to the technology competition between the United States and China. Washington has restricted exports of advanced chips to prevent Beijing from acquiring computing power that could help it match or surpass U.S. capabilities.
Nvidia defended its chief executive's dealings with Alice Huang and said customers do not receive sensitive company information.
"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.'s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," company spokesperson John Rizzo told the Times.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who became a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and Nvidia customer.
Toward the end of the Biden administration, the Commerce Department began investigating suspicions that Megaspeed was helping China circumvent U.S. restrictions on access to Nvidia's computing technology, the Times reported. Nvidia said its own investigation found no evidence that Megaspeed was smuggling chips.
Surveillance of Alice Huang subsequently led U.S. officials to conclude she was providing information to Beijing. Her relationship with Jensen Huang raised questions about whether she could obtain sensitive information about Nvidia or Trump's thinking on chip exports, according to the report.
Jensen Huang has become an influential advocate for easing restrictions on chip sales to China. Trump was wary of disrupting sales that help drive the economy and stock market or further complicating trade relations with Beijing, the Times reported.
When Trump was initially briefed, officials did not believe Jensen Huang knew Alice Huang was gathering intelligence for China. The Times said it was unclear whether intelligence agencies had since changed that assessment.
Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing, a warning sometimes given to Americans targeted by foreign intelligence services. Such warnings can risk alerting a surveillance target, although the Times could not determine whether that concern explained the decision in this case.
Rizzo said Nvidia was confident the government would notify the company if it believed someone posed a threat to American industry.
Megaspeed said it retained outside counsel to investigate the allegations and informed the U.S. government that it would cooperate. Alice Huang did not respond to requests for comment, and her current role at the company remains unclear.
The White House, CIA, and National Security Agency declined to comment. Chinese Embassy spokesperson Liu Chang accused the United States of pursuing "groundless smears and slanders."
